**On Desire Paths**

There is a word for the dirt track that appears diagonally across a lawn where the sidewalk makes a right angle. Landscape architects call it a desire path. Sometimes a desire line. The name is almost too good—it sounds like something out of a poem, but it's a technical term, the kind of phrase that shows up in municipal planning documents next to budget figures for mulch.

A desire path is the record of a disagreement. On one side is the person who drew the plan: the paved walkway goes here, at ninety degrees, because the grid is clean and the drainage works and the drawing looked right. On the other side is everyone who ever walked there and thought, without thinking, *no*. Each of them shaved a few seconds off their route. None of them intended to build anything. But feet are patient, and grass is not, and after a season there it is: a brown seam through the green, a sentence written by hundreds of people who never met.

I find these paths moving in a way that's a little hard to justify. Part of it is that they're honest. A desire path cannot lie about where people want to go. It's not a survey, not a focus group, not a comment card where you say what you think you ought to want. It's the accumulated residue of actual behavior, and behavior is stubborn. You can put up a sign. You can plant a hedge. People will walk around the hedge and wear a new path, slightly wider, with a small detour that itself becomes permanent.

Some universities have figured this out and now wait. They open a new quad with no paved walkways at all, just grass, and let the students cross it for a year. Then they pave wherever the dirt appeared. This strikes me as one of the wiser things an institution can do, and it's wise precisely because it involves an admission: *we don't know where you'll want to walk, and we've stopped pretending we do.* The plan comes after the life, not before it. The designer's job becomes less about dictating and more about noticing, and then honoring what was noticed with a bit of concrete.

But I don't want to make this too tidy, because desire paths are also a little sad. They're compromises worn into the ground. Every one of them represents a small failure of imagination somewhere upstream—someone who could have asked, or looked, or simply walked the route themselves before drawing it. And the path that results is never quite what anyone would have chosen either. It's muddy in the rain. It kills the grass. It's a shortcut, and shortcuts have a certain bleak efficiency about them; they get you there faster but they don't make you glad to be walking.

Still, there's something in the gap between the plan and the path that I keep returning to. It shows up everywhere once you start looking. The recipe says one thing and the cook, after the third time, does another. The software has a menu with fourteen options and everyone uses two. The building has a grand front entrance and the staff all come in through the loading dock because it's closer to the parking. Language itself is mostly desire paths: the grammarians draw the sidewalk and the speakers cut across, and after enough centuries the diagonal *is* the grammar.

What's interesting is that the path never announces itself. No single walker decides to make it. If you asked any one of them, they'd say they were just going to the library. The path is what philosophers sometimes call an emergent thing—it exists at a level above any individual's intention, built out of intentions that were all pointed somewhere else. That's the ordinary miracle of it. A road that nobody designed and everybody built.

I think about this in relation to how we tell stories about cities and institutions and traditions. We like a founder. We like someone who stood on the hill and pointed and said *there*. And sometimes that's how it happened. But a great deal of what we live inside—the streets of older cities, the customs of a workplace, the idioms of a language, the way a family celebrates a holiday—is closer to a desire path. It was worn, not drawn. It's the sum of a great many small choices that were each about something else, sedimented until they looked like a decision.

There's a modesty in accepting that, and also a kind of freedom. If the path was worn rather than decreed, then it can be worn differently. The grass grows back with surprising speed once people stop walking on it. A path that looks permanent is really just a path that's still in use.

I'll admit I also just like the way they look. From above—a satellite photo, a high window—desire paths turn a campus or a park into a kind of drawing, all these lines converging on doors and bus stops and the one bench in the shade. They map wanting. They show where the coffee is. They show the invisible geography of a place, which is not the geography of its plan but the geography of its use: where people actually are, when, and how much they'd rather not go the long way.

The next time you see one, notice the width. A narrow path means a few determined walkers. A wide one, with the grass gone entirely and the dirt packed hard, means a whole community quietly overruling somebody's drawing, day after day, for years. It's not a protest. Nobody's angry. It's just feet, doing what feet do, which is go toward what they want by the shortest honest route.

And someday, if the place is lucky, someone will come along with a wheelbarrow and a bag of gravel and make it official. The plan will finally agree with the path. Which is, I think, the best order for those two things to arrive in.
